transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doc, I guess what brings me in is... I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting. Like my heart follow-up appointments. I missed one recently, and I was supposed to call the clinic back, but I completely forgot to do that, too. Which is a shame because my heart doctor is a real nice guy, always wears these ridiculous bright bowties. I asked him about 'em once and he said his daughter makes them for him. She lives out in Oregon, I think. Or maybe Washington? Somewhere out west where it rains a lot, anyway. My brother lived in Seattle for a few years back in the eighties, said he couldn't stand the drizzle. 

But, uh... where was I? Oh, right, forgetting things. Yeah, it's not just the clinic. I'll go over to help my neighbor with a repair job—he's fixing up this old cherry red Chevy truck, beautiful body on it but the carburetor is an absolute nightmare, we've been tinkering with it for weeks—and I'll show up without the right tools. I'll walk all the way over there and realize I didn't bring the socket set I needed. It's just... I don't know, it's getting frustrating.
Have you struggled with this kind of forgetfulness since you were younger, or is this something that's new for you, say within the last several months to a year?

Since I was younger? You know, I’m really not sure. I haven't really thought about it like that. When I was younger, things were just... different. I mean, back in high school, I worked down at this hardware store on Main Street. Old man Higgins ran the place. He was a real piece of work, let me tell you. Used to keep all the loose nails in these giant wooden barrels, and you had to weigh 'em out for the customers on this big, heavy iron scale. 

They really don't make scales like that anymore, do they? Everything is digital now. I actually just bought one of those little digital scales for the kitchen a few weeks ago because my wife wanted to start making her own bread. Sourdough, I think it was. You have to feed the sourdough starter every single day, which honestly just seems like having another pet. We already have a golden retriever, Buster, and he eats enough for three dogs, I swear. He got into the trash last week and... 

But, uh... wait. What were we talking about? Oh, right, my memory. Yeah, I honestly couldn't tell you if this is a new thing or if I've always been this way. It's hard to say.
Has your wife or anyone else close to you mentioned noticing this forgetfulness, and if so, do they feel it's gotten worse over the past several months?

My wife? Hmm, I don't know if she's said it's gotten worse exactly. She gets annoyed when I forget things, sure, but I don't know about worse. Like yesterday, she sent me to the hardware store for some special potting soil she likes, and I came back with birdseed instead. She’s got this whole garden setup in the backyard now. Planted all these hydrangeas along the back fence. 

Did you know they change color depending on what's in the dirt? You can put old coffee grounds in there to make the flowers blue. Or maybe it makes them pink, I can never remember. We save all our coffee grounds in this little tin can by the sink. It’s an old Maxwell House can, the metal kind, you know? My dad used to keep his fishing worms in a can just like that. We'd go out to Miller's Pond every Sunday when I was a kid... caught a largemouth bass as big as my arm out there once. Fought like crazy. Broke my favorite rod, actually. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, my wife. Yeah, she complains about me forgetting the groceries or the tools or the appointments, but I honestly couldn't tell you if she thinks it's worse now than it was a year ago. She's always got something to say about my listening skills, so it all kind of blends together.
Besides forgetting things, have you noticed any new difficulty with tasks like managing your finances, following instructions, or finding your way in places you know well?

Finances and instructions? Well, I wouldn't say I'm getting lost or anything like that. I know my way around town just fine. I've lived here for... gosh, going on forty years now. We bought the house back in '84, right before the big blizzard. I tell you, I've never seen snow like that since. It was piled up all the way to the gutters! We had this old snowblower, a Toro I think, and it just choked on the stuff. Had to shovel the whole driveway by hand. My back was out for a week. 

But, uh, paying bills and things? No, I haven't noticed any new trouble with that. I mean, my wife usually handles the checkbook anyway. She's got this whole system with color-coded folders. Red for utilities, blue for medical, green for the house stuff. She tried to explain it to me once, but honestly, I just let her do it. She used to work as a bookkeeper for a small shipping company downtown, so she's good with numbers. They shipped mostly auto parts, I think. Or maybe it was farm equipment? I remember she brought home this giant calendar once with all these tractors on it. I hung it up in the garage for years.

So, yeah, no new problems with that kind of stuff, really. Just the forgetting.
Did your memory trouble start or get noticeably worse around the time of any specific health event, like a heart problem, hospital stay, surgery, or a change in your medications?

A health event? Well, actually, yeah, now that you mention it. It's been causing real trouble for about a year and two months now. That's when I had my cardiac scare. Scared the living daylights out of my wife, I tell you. I was just out in the garage, trying to fix the lawnmower. It's a John Deere, one of those riding ones, you know? Great machine, but the carburetor gets gunked up if you don't winterize it right. I usually use that fuel stabilizer stuff, comes in a little red bottle, but I guess I forgot that year. 

Anyway, the doctor told me I had to cut way back on my walking and all my projects around the house. Said I needed to take it easy. Taking it easy! I've never been one to just sit around. Used to keep me settled, you know, always having something to tinker with or a place to walk to. Buster loved those walks, too. We'd go all the way down to the old railroad tracks. They pulled the tracks up years ago, though. Turned it into one of those walking trails. Paved the whole thing. It's nice, I suppose, but I kind of miss the old wooden ties. They smelled like creosote in the summer. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, the memory thing. Yeah, it definitely got worse after that heart scare when I had to stop doing all my usual stuff. About a year and two months ago, like I said.
During that cardiac scare a year and two months ago, did you lose consciousness or have your heart actually stop, or were you told you went without oxygen for any period of time?

Lose consciousness? No, no, nothing like that. My heart didn't stop, either. I didn't pass out or go without oxygen, thank goodness. I was just feeling this awful tightness, you know? Like someone had parked a truck on my chest. An old Ford pickup, maybe. My uncle had an old F-150 when I was growing up. Two-tone, blue and white. Beautiful truck. We used to ride in the back of it down to the county fair every August. You can't do that anymore, of course. Safety rules and all that. They make you buckle up just to back out of the driveway now. 

But no, to answer your question, I was awake the whole time. Just felt terrible and had to go to the hospital. They put me in this gown that wouldn't tie right in the back. I hate those gowns. Drafty, you know? But no, my heart didn't stop or anything.
Since that heart scare a year and two months ago, would you say your memory has been steadily getting worse and worse, or has it stayed about the same level of trouble since then?

Steadily getting worse? Gosh, I don't know if I'd say worse and worse. I mean, it's definitely been a nuisance since then, but I think it's mostly just stayed about the same level of bad since the scare. It's just so frustrating, you know? Not being able to rely on my own head. 

It reminds me of this old pocket watch my grandfather gave me. Beautiful thing, gold plated, had his initials engraved on the back. E.J.H. Edward James Harrison. He was a watchmaker, actually. Had a little shop down on Main Street, right next to the bakery. Oh, the smell of that bakery! They made these cinnamon rolls that were as big as your head. We'd go there every Sunday after church. My mother always said it would spoil my lunch, but my grandfather would sneak me one anyway. He used to say a little sugar never hurt a growing boy. 

But anyway, that pocket watch... it just stopped keeping time right one day. It would run, but it was always a few minutes off, no matter how much you wound it. Just stayed that way. Never got worse, never got better. Kind of like my memory right now, I guess. Just consistently... off.
How do you feel about these memory lapses—do they worry you or bother you emotionally, or do you find yourself not too concerned about them?

Bother me? Oh, it bothers me a lot. It’s incredibly frustrating. You know, you spend your whole life being sharp as a tack, and then suddenly you can't remember why you walked into the kitchen. It makes me worry, sure. I mean, my aunt Shirley had memory problems, but hers was different. She started putting her car keys in the refrigerator. The refrigerator! Can you imagine? We found them right next to the mayonnaise one day. Hellmann's, I think it was. Shirley always insisted on Hellmann's. Said the store brand tasted like plastic. We used to make these turkey sandwiches after Thanksgiving with that mayo, and she’d put cranberry sauce right on the bread. It sounds strange, but it was actually delicious. You had to use the canned cranberry sauce, though, the kind that keeps the shape of the can when it slides out. I always liked slicing it into perfect little circles. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, the memory lapses. Yeah, they definitely worry me. I just hate feeling like I'm losing my grip on things, you know? It's really upsetting.

Since your heart scare, if someone teaches you something new—like a new recipe step, a new route, or a new person's name—are you able to remember it later that same day, or does it slip away almost right after you learn it?

New things? Oh, well... it really depends, I guess. I haven't really tried to learn a new recipe lately. My wife does most of the cooking now. She makes this incredible meatloaf. It's got this glaze on top, sort of sweet and tangy. I think she puts brown sugar and ketchup in it. Ketchup is funny, isn't it? When I was a kid, we used to put ketchup on our scrambled eggs. My brother Tommy—he's the one who moved out to Arizona—he would drown his eggs in it. Just a sea of red on the plate. He always said the eggs were just a vehicle for the ketchup. Tommy was a character. He used to collect bottle caps. Had boxes and boxes of them in the garage. 

But, learning new things... I don't know, it's hard to say. I guess I haven't really noticed if it slips away right away or not. I just haven't had to learn much new stuff lately, you know? Just trying to keep track of the old stuff!
Aside from the memory lapses, have you noticed any new difficulty concentrating, planning tasks, or finding the right words when you speak?

Concentrating? Yeah, actually, that's been... well, it's definitely been tricky. I can sit down at the bridge table, or like, at a Fix-It Friends planning meeting—that's this group I'm in, we fix up broken stuff for folks around town. Mostly small appliances, toasters, lamps, that sort of thing. I fixed this beautiful Tiffany-style lamp last week. The stained glass on it was just gorgeous. Lots of greens and blues. My wife loves stained glass. We went to this church in Europe once, oh, forty years ago, and the windows were just breathtaking. The way the light hit the floor, it looked like a giant kaleidoscope. We bought a little glass suncatcher in the gift shop that day, and it still hangs in our kitchen window. It casts these little rainbows on the linoleum when the sun sets. 

But, uh, anyway, I'll be sitting there at the bridge table or the meeting, meaning to pay close attention to whoever is talking. I really do try. But after a little while, my mind just slides off. It just wanders completely away, and suddenly I realize I missed half of what was said. So I guess my concentration isn't doing so great either.
Do you remember the details of what happened right before, during, and right after your cardiac scare, or is there a specific period of time around that event that's just missing from your memory?

The details? Well, I don't think there's any missing time, really. I remember it happening. I remember the paramedics coming in. One of them, this young kid, he had the thickest mustache I've ever seen on a guy his age. Looked like a woolly caterpillar crawling right across his lip! You just don't see mustaches like that much anymore. Back in the seventies, sure, everyone had one. I had one! My wife hated it, though. She said it tickled too much when I kissed her. She actually made me shave it off right before our big trip to Hawaii in '78. Oh, Hawaii was just beautiful. We went to Maui and drove that Road to Hana. Talk about winding roads! I thought I was going to be sick, going around all those sharp little curves, but the waterfalls at the end were just... spectacular. We bought these little carved wooden turtles at a roadside stand from this local fellow. He carved them right there with a pocket knife. I still have mine on my nightstand. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, the heart thing. Yeah, no, I don't think I forgot any of it. I remember the whole ordeal pretty clearly, unfortunately.
I'd like to do a quick memory test: I'm going to say three words—apple, table, and coin—please remember them, and I'll ask you to repeat them back to me in about five minutes.

Apple, table, coin. Got it. Apple... you know, we used to have an apple tree in the backyard of the house I grew up in. A big old Macintosh tree. The apples were so tart, they'd make your jaw ache if you ate them before they were ready. But my mom, she would make the most incredible pies with them. She had this special crust recipe, used lard instead of butter. Nobody uses lard anymore, do they? It's all about health food now. Kale and quinoa and whatever else. I tried quinoa once at my niece's wedding. Tasted like wet sand. She had this whole vegan spread. The wedding was out in a barn, which is popular now, I guess. We were all sweating through our suits. But the band was good! They played a lot of old Motown hits. I love Motown. The Temptations, Smokey Robinson... they don't make music like that anymore. 

What were the words again? Apple... table... and... coin. Right. I'll try to keep them in my head.
Now, can you tell me the three words I asked you to remember a few minutes ago?

The three words... right. Okay, let me think. Um... apple. Yes, apple was the first one. Because of the tree, right. And then... oh boy. Was it... no, not chair. Table! Apple, table. A table... you know, I built a coffee table once. Back when I had a full workshop in the garage. Used solid oak. Heavy as a tank, that thing was. My son still has it in his living room. He’s got three kids now, boys, and they climb all over it like it’s a jungle gym. They’re wild, those boys. Always running around, breaking things. One of them threw a baseball right through the front window last summer. Shattered everywhere. Cost him a pretty penny to get that fixed. Glass repair isn't cheap these days. Nothing is cheap these days, really. Have you seen the price of eggs lately? It’s highway robbery. 

But, uh... the last word. Apple, table... and... gosh. I know it was something small. A button? No, that's not it. I'm sorry, Doc, the third one just slipped right out of my head. What was it again?

Things from years ago? No, no, I don't think so. My memory for the old days is sharp as a tack. I can remember the exact color of the first car I ever bought. It was a '67 Mustang, cherry red, with these gorgeous white leather seats. Oh, I loved that car. I used to wash it every Sunday morning, rain or shine. Used this special wax, smelled like coconuts. I bought it from a guy named Frank who ran a little dealership down on 4th Street. Frank always wore these loud plaid suits, even in the dead of summer. He had a glass eye, too. You could never quite tell if he was looking at you or the car. They tore that dealership down years ago, put up a strip mall. Got a dry cleaner, a pizza place... the pizza's not bad, actually. Thin crust. I prefer a thick crust, myself, like the kind they make in Chicago. I went to Chicago once for a conference. Coldest wind I ever felt in my life, coming right off the lake. It cuts right through your coat, no matter how thick it is. 

So, yeah, the old stuff? I remember it all just fine. It's just the new things that don't seem to stick.

doctor.intent: Identify the primary reason for the visit
doctor.question: Hi, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t, like heart follow-up appointments, calling the clinic back, or showing up with the right tools for a repair job.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S009.

patient.answer:
Well, doc, I guess what brings me in is... I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting. Like my heart follow-up appointments. I missed one recently, and I was supposed to call the clinic back, but I completely forgot to do that, too. Which is a shame because my heart doctor is a real nice guy, always wears these ridiculous bright bowties. I asked him about 'em once and he said his daughter makes them for him. She lives out in Oregon, I think. Or maybe Washington? Somewhere out west where it rains a lot, anyway. My brother lived in Seattle for a few years back in the eighties, said he couldn't stand the drizzle. 

But, uh... where was I? Oh, right, forgetting things. Yeah, it's not just the clinic. I'll go over to help my neighbor with a repair job—he's fixing up this old cherry red Chevy truck, beautiful body on it but the carburetor is an absolute nightmare, we've been tinkering with it for weeks—and I'll show up without the right tools. I'll walk all the way over there and realize I didn't bring the socket set I needed. It's just... I don't know, it's getting frustrating.
